```{python}
import pandas as pd

# Week 1's data collection is done and cleaned -- reads the same stable
# week1_reaction_times_final.csv the Week 2 deck uses, not a synthetic
# placeholder or a live in-progress Google Sheet. This used to be two
# separate files (week3.qmd on synthetic data, week3-live.qmd on the live
# sheet) -- collapsed back into this one file once real class data existed,
# same reasoning as Week 2 (see CLAUDE.md's "Single deck per week" entry).
df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stevenolanecon/7002LBSAI/main/data/week1_reaction_times_final.csv")

if 'name' in df.columns and 'student_name' not in df.columns:
    df = df.rename(columns={'name': 'student_name'})
if 'caffeine' not in df.columns:
    df['caffeine'] = 'Unknown'
df['caffeine'] = df['caffeine'].fillna('Unknown')

# week1_reaction_times_final.csv's own name/student_name values are already
# anonymised at the source (Student 1, Student 2, ... — real names were
# never in this file to begin with, only in the live Google Sheet and
# Week 1's own already-published content).

# finger_mm may not exist on older submissions — coerce and tolerate absence
if 'finger_mm' not in df.columns:
    df['finger_mm'] = None
df['finger_mm'] = pd.to_numeric(df['finger_mm'], errors='coerce')

students = sorted(df['student_name'].unique().tolist(), key=lambda s: int(s.split()[-1]))

# One row per student: mean reaction time, device, caffeine, finger length
student_summary = (
    df.groupby('student_name')
    .agg(mean_rt=('reaction_time_ms', 'mean'),
         device=('device', 'first'),
         caffeine=('caffeine', 'first'),
         finger_mm=('finger_mm', 'first'))
    .reset_index()
    .round(1)
)

# Real data-quality issue, found while building this deck: 5 of our real
# students' finger_mm values are physically implausible for an adult index
# finger (roughly 60-100mm) -- 3 far too small (under 10mm, consistent with
# being entered in centimetres rather than millimetres) and 2 far too large
# (700-900mm, consistent with an extra typed digit). Left uncorrected, these
# 5 points alone were driving the covariance/correlation numbers this
# session computes downstream (0.36/66,893 with them in, vs ~0.18-0.20/
# ~1,400-1,500 once corrected -- a real difference in what the slide
# teaches, not a cosmetic one). Rather than silently fix it, this is turned
# into the student task below ("Task — what's wrong with our finger-length
# data?") -- students see the raw, anonymised values first and decide for
# themselves what's wrong and what to do about it, before the actual
# resolution (impute, not drop) is revealed. finger_mm_raw is kept
# unmodified for that task's own table; finger_mm itself is corrected here
# so every later slide (binning, the scatter, covariance, correlation)
# already uses the imputed values, matching the resolution the task reveals.
FINGER_LOW_MM, FINGER_HIGH_MM = 40, 150
student_summary['finger_mm_raw'] = student_summary['finger_mm']
student_summary['finger_mm'] = student_summary['finger_mm_raw'].apply(
    lambda x: x * 10 if pd.notna(x) and x < FINGER_LOW_MM
    else (x / 10 if pd.notna(x) and x > FINGER_HIGH_MM else x)
)

# Order-scrambled view of the raw finger-length values for the task slide —
# student_name is already the anonymised Student-N label from above; rows
# are shuffled (not shown in Student-1..N order) so the 5 bad values aren't
# trivially obvious just from their position in the list.
finger_task_rows = (
    student_summary[['student_name', 'finger_mm_raw']]
    .rename(columns={'finger_mm_raw': 'finger_mm'})
    .sample(frac=1, random_state=7)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

# Joint device x caffeine counts, one row per student (not per trial)
students_df = df.drop_duplicates('student_name')
joint_table = (
    students_df.groupby(['device', 'caffeine']).size()
    .reset_index(name='count')
)

# NaN (e.g. missing finger_mm) is not valid JSON. All ojs_define() values share
# one JSON payload, so a single stray NaN anywhere breaks every variable in the
# call — clean each one before handing it over.
df_clean = df.astype(object).where(df.notna(), None)
student_summary_clean = student_summary.astype(object).where(student_summary.notna(), None)
joint_table_clean = joint_table.astype(object).where(joint_table.notna(), None)
finger_task_rows_clean = finger_task_rows.astype(object).where(finger_task_rows.notna(), None)

ojs_define(
    data              = df_clean.to_dict(orient='records'),
    students          = students,
    student_summary   = student_summary_clean.to_dict(orient='records'),
    joint_table       = joint_table_clean.to_dict(orient='records'),
    finger_task_rows  = finger_task_rows_clean.to_dict(orient='records'),
)
```

```{python}
import numpy as np

# ── A second, separate, deliberately SYNTHETIC (not our class data) dataset
# for the scatter / bin-scatter / log-transform teaching sequence
# ("Scatterplot and bin-scatter", "Does logging reaction time help?").
# Deliberately NOT finger length -- students are set a task later to build
# exactly that scatter themselves, so the worked example here uses a
# different x (a plausible, separate driver of reaction time: hours of
# sleep the night before), generated to reliably show what logging is
# *for*. Tried and rejected assigning made-up sleep hours to our own real
# reaction-time data instead (2026-09-29): with no genuine relationship
# between the two, raw and logged R^2 came out identical (~0.025 each) --
# logging can only sharpen a relationship that's actually there, it can't
# invent one, so this has to stay a fully synthetic illustration.
#
# Sizing history, each round verified numerically before committing, not
# just eyeballed: v1 used a handful of moderately slow trials -- real but
# too subtle (R^2 improved only ~1.8x, main cluster still occupied ~60% of
# either axis). v2 used a few *severe* outliers on a 66-point, ~380ms-
# baseline sample -- better (~22% vs ~39% of axis, R^2 0.10 -> 0.24, a
# 2.4x gap) but still not dramatic. v3 (current): more points (150, so 2-3
# extreme outliers are a smaller share of the total and don't wreck the
# log fit's own R^2 the way they did at n=66), a steeper underlying slope,
# tighter non-outlier noise, and only 2 but much more severe outliers
# (2000-2800ms against a ~150-300ms main cluster). This pushes raw R^2 down
# to ~0.02 -- genuinely undetectable, not just weak -- while log R^2 holds
# at ~0.22, a qualitative "can't see it" vs "can see it" contrast rather
# than a "weaker" vs "stronger" one. Confirmed the bin-scatter's own bins
# still average at least 12 trials each at this larger n (previously 4+).
np.random.seed(21)
n_sleep = 150
sleep_hours = np.round(np.random.uniform(4, 9.5, n_sleep), 1)
_a, _b, _sigma = 5.95, 0.12, 0.05
_log_rt = _a - _b * sleep_hours + np.random.normal(0, _sigma, n_sleep)
sleep_rt = np.clip(np.exp(_log_rt), 150, None).round(1)

# Two severe "very bad day" trials -- the real-world reason reaction time
# has a long right tail, deliberately extreme here so the raw-vs-logged
# contrast is unmistakable rather than subtle. Not the first seed tried:
# seed_out=5 put both outliers in the same 1h sleep bin, producing a
# visible spike on "The bin-scatter" that undercut that slide's own point
# about bins being robust to individual lapses; seed_out=9 fixed the spike
# but the bin-scatter's own mean still wasn't monotonically decreasing.
# seed_out=15 puts both outliers at the low-sleep end (4.4-4.6h) --
# narratively coherent (a bad night's sleep coinciding with a bad trial
# isn't a stretch) -- and gives a genuinely clean, monotonically
# decreasing bin-scatter with an even stronger R^2 contrast (raw ~0.08,
# log ~0.35), confirmed against real computed output before committing.
_rng = np.random.default_rng(15)
_n_out = 2
_idx_out = _rng.choice(n_sleep, _n_out, replace=False)
sleep_hours = np.concatenate([sleep_hours, sleep_hours[_idx_out]])
sleep_rt    = np.concatenate([sleep_rt, _rng.uniform(2000, 2800, _n_out).round(1)])

sleep_scatter_data = [
    {'sleep_hours': float(sleep_hours[i]), 'reaction_time_ms': float(sleep_rt[i])}
    for i in range(len(sleep_hours))
]

ojs_define(sleep_scatter_data = sleep_scatter_data)
```

```{python}
# ── A third, SYNTHETIC illustration: hours awake before the test vs.
# reaction time, built to show a clearly visible strong positive
# relationship right after our own (weak) finger-length scatter. Same n as
# the class (24) so it reads as "a class like ours, if the relationship were
# real". Seed 3 chosen after checking seeds 1-14: r = 0.89 -- strong, but not
# implausibly perfect. Used twice: shown without its correlation after
# "Finger length vs. reaction time — our data" (the number is revealed live
# in class), then brought back after "Task — calculate the correlation" with
# its covariance and SDs stated, for students to compute r themselves.
_rng_awake = np.random.default_rng(3)
awake_hours = np.round(_rng_awake.uniform(2, 18, 24), 1)
awake_rt = np.round(260 + 14 * awake_hours + _rng_awake.normal(0, 30, 24), 0)
awake_data = [{'hours_awake': float(x), 'reaction_time_ms': float(y)}
              for x, y in zip(awake_hours, awake_rt)]
# Stated to students rounded, so the answer is computed from the same
# rounded figures they'll use -- no mismatch between their number and ours.
awake_stats = {
    'n': int(len(awake_hours)),
    'cov': round(float(np.cov(awake_hours, awake_rt)[0, 1]), 1),
    'sd_x': round(float(awake_hours.std(ddof=1)), 2),
    'sd_y': round(float(awake_rt.std(ddof=1)), 1),
}
awake_stats['corr'] = round(awake_stats['cov'] / (awake_stats['sd_x'] * awake_stats['sd_y']), 2)

ojs_define(awake_data = awake_data, awake_stats = awake_stats)
```

```{python}
# ── Practice and independence illustrations (all SYNTHETIC, labelled as such
# on-slide). Added 2026-10-06 when the latent-variables section was cut to
# make room for more in-class practice on the assessed core (conditional
# probability, covariance/correlation) and for Gabor Ch. 4's dependence /
# mean-dependence / correlation distinction.

# (1) "Guess the correlation": four 40-point clouds, seeds chosen so each
# sample r lands within 0.003 of its target (0.9, 0.5, 0.0, -0.6). Shown in
# a shuffled order (A-D) so the targets aren't in an obvious sequence.
def _cloud(target, seed, n=40):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x = r.normal(0, 1, n)
    y = target * x + np.sqrt(1 - target**2) * r.normal(0, 1, n)
    return x, y
_guess_specs = [('A', 0.5, 150), ('B', -0.6, 22), ('C', 0.9, 191), ('D', 0.0, 117)]
guess_data, guess_r = [], {}
for lab, tgt, seed in _guess_specs:
    x, y = _cloud(tgt, seed)
    guess_r[lab] = round(float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]), 2)
    guess_data += [{'panel': lab, 'x': float(a), 'y': float(b)} for a, b in zip(x, y)]

# (2) Four kinds of (in)dependence, Gabor Ch. 4. x is built from mirrored
# pairs (u, -u) and, for the three "r = 0" panels, each pair shares the same
# noise -- so y is an even function of x and the sample correlation is
# exactly zero, not just "close to zero by luck". Keeps the slide's point
# clean: these three really do have r = 0, yet only one is independent.
_r = np.random.default_rng(11)
_u = _r.uniform(0, 2, 100)
_xs = np.concatenate([_u, -_u])
_e = np.tile(_r.normal(0, 1, 100), 2)
_e_ind = np.tile(_r.normal(0, 1, 100), 2)
_dep_panels = {
    '1. Independent':                   _e_ind,
    '2. Linear: mean-dependent':        0.8 * _xs + 0.6 * _r.normal(0, 1, 200),
    '3. U-shape: mean-dependent, r = 0': _xs**2 - 4/3 + 0.4 * _e,
    '4. Fan: spread depends on x, r = 0': _e * (0.15 + 0.6 * np.abs(_xs)),
}
dep_data, dep_r = [], {}
for name, ys in _dep_panels.items():
    dep_r[name] = round(float(np.corrcoef(_xs, ys)[0, 1]), 2) + 0.0
    dep_data += [{'panel': name, 'x': float(a), 'y': float(b)} for a, b in zip(_xs, ys)]

# (3) Five students, small integer data chosen so covariance and correlation
# come out clean by hand: Cov = 8, SD_x = SD_y = sqrt(10), Corr = 0.8.
five_hours  = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
five_scores = [3, 7, 5, 11, 9]

ojs_define(guess_data = guess_data, guess_r = guess_r,
           dep_data = dep_data, dep_r = dep_r,
           five_hours = five_hours, five_scores = five_scores)
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
{
  // Generic "shrink on reveal" wiring, used by every chart wrapped as
  // `:::: {.shrink-on-reveal data-frag="some-fragment-id" style="--large-height:...;--small-height:...;--shrink-scale:..."}`
  // Each chart renders large while its named fragment is hidden, then
  // shrinks smoothly to make room the moment that fragment is revealed.
  // Sizes live entirely in each wrapper's own inline style — this cell only
  // handles show/hide, once, for every wrapper on the page, so adding a new
  // chart to this pattern never means touching this cell.
  const wrapperFor = (fragId) => document.querySelector(`.shrink-on-reveal[data-frag="${fragId}"]`)
  const syncAll = () => {
    document.querySelectorAll('.fragment[id]').forEach(frag =>
      wrapperFor(frag.id)?.classList.toggle('is-small', frag.classList.contains('visible'))
    )
  }

  // Sets each wrapper's correct starting state immediately, including on a
  // reload or direct navigation to a slide whose fragment is already shown.
  syncAll()

  // PDF export (decktape / reveal.js print-pdf mode) rebuilds the slide DOM
  // rather than toggling each fragment's class in place, so watch the whole
  // document and re-sync on any change -- same fix as Week 2 (see its own
  // comment for how this was diagnosed).
  const observer = new MutationObserver(syncAll)
  observer.observe(document.body, { childList: true, subtree: true, attributes: true, attributeFilter: ['class'] })

  Reveal.on('fragmentshown', (event) => {
    wrapperFor(event.fragment.id)?.classList.add('is-small')
  })
  Reveal.on('fragmenthidden', (event) => {
    wrapperFor(event.fragment.id)?.classList.remove('is-small')
  })
}
```

```{ojs}
// Screen readers walk into an SVG's own children unless told otherwise --
// Observable Plot gives every mark and axis tick its own generic aria-label
// ("dot", "x-axis tick", ...), so without this wrapper a screen reader reads
// through dozens of those instead of one meaningful description. Wrapping in
// a role="img" container and hiding the SVG itself (aria-hidden) makes the
// wrapper's one aria-label the whole story. Same helper as wk1/wk2.
function accessibleChart(node, label) {
  node.setAttribute("aria-hidden", "true")
  const wrapper = document.createElement("div")
  wrapper.setAttribute("role", "img")
  wrapper.setAttribute("aria-label", label)
  wrapper.appendChild(node)
  return wrapper
}
```

## A shortcut for HR

::: {.instructions-box}
The reaction-time test works, but it takes ten trials per person to administer. HR wants something faster: **"find us a quick physical measurement that predicts reaction time, and we'll screen candidates on that instead."**
:::

::: {.fragment}
That's why we collected **index finger length** back in Week 1.

Is it a fast, reliable stand-in for the real test? Today gives us the tools to answer that properly — and the discipline not to answer it too quickly.
:::

---

## When y met x

---

## The y and the x

Much of data analysis is about comparing values of a **y** variable across values of an **x** variable — uncovering patterns of association.

- By convention, **y** is the variable we're interested in; **x** is what we compare across
- **Goal 1 — prediction:** use x to predict y, without needing to know *why*
- **Goal 2 — causal effect:** learn what would happen to y if we *changed* x

::: {.fragment}
HR's proxy-test idea is a **prediction** goal, dressed up as if it were free of that distinction. Keep watching for where the two goals get blurred.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), *Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy*, Ch. 4
:::

## Association

Two variables are **associated** when the values of y tend to differ across values of x: knowing x tells you something about y.

- **Positive association:** higher values of x go with higher values of y, on average
- **Negative association:** higher values of x go with lower values of y, on average
- **No association:** y looks the same whatever the value of x (the variables are **independent**)

::: {.fragment}
Everything today measures association: conditional probabilities, conditional means, covariance and correlation are all ways of describing *how* y differs across x.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Association is not causation.** An association tells you two things move together in the data. On its own, it doesn't tell you whether changing x would change y. We come back to that at the end of the session.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

---

## Conditional probability

---

## Conditioning on x {.smaller}

**Comparison → conditioning.** Comparing y by values of x means we **condition** y on x — x is the **conditioning variable**, y is the **outcome variable**.

Worked example: 20 students, 12 use a Phone, and 9 of those 12 had caffeine.

```{=html}
<table style="width:70%;margin:12px auto 18px auto;border-collapse:collapse;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.9em;">
  <thead><tr style="background:#1a1a2e;color:white;">

    <th scope="col" style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;">Caffeine</th>

      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;color:#457b9d;">3</td>

    <tr style="background:#fafafa;border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">

      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;color:#457b9d;">6</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">8</td>
    </tr>

      <td style="padding:7px 18px;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">Total</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">11</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">9</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#e9edf1;"><span class="fragment highlight-current-red" data-fragment-index="3">20</span></td>
    </tr>

```

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**Joint probability** — the chance both things happen together: $P(A \text{ and } B)$
:::

[Here: $P(\text{Caffeine and Phone}) =$]{.fragment fragment-index=2} [$\frac{9}{20} = 0.45$ — 9 of all 20 students]{.fragment fragment-index=3}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
**Conditional probability** — the chance of A, *restricted to* the cases where B happened: $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}$
:::

[Here: $P(\text{Caffeine} \mid \text{Phone}) =$]{.fragment fragment-index=5} [$\frac{9}{12} = 0.75$ — 9 of the 12 phone users]{.fragment fragment-index=6}

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

## Independence

```{=html}
<table style="width:70%;margin:12px auto 18px auto;border-collapse:collapse;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.9em;">
  <thead><tr style="background:#1a1a2e;color:white;">
    <th scope="col" style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:left;">Device \ Caffeine</th>
    <th scope="col" style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;">Caffeine</th>
    <th scope="col" style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;">No caffeine</th>
    <th scope="col" style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;background:#2d6a4f;">Total</th>
  </tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr style="border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;font-weight:700;">Phone</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;color:#457b9d;">9</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;color:#457b9d;">3</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">12</td>
    </tr>
    <tr style="background:#fafafa;border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;font-weight:700;">Laptop</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;color:#457b9d;">2</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;color:#457b9d;">6</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">8</td>
    </tr>
    <tr style="border-top:2px solid #1a1a2e;">
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">Total</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">11</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">9</td>
      <td style="padding:7px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#e9edf1;">20</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
```

::: {.fragment}
**Independence** — A and B are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other: $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$. If so, $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$; if not, use $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A \mid B) \times P(B)$, which always holds.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Here: overall $P(\text{Caffeine}) = \frac{11}{20} = 0.55$, but $P(\text{Caffeine} \mid \text{Phone}) = \frac{9}{12} = 0.75$ — **not equal, so not independent.** The shortcut would give $\frac{12}{20} \times \frac{11}{20} = 0.6 \times 0.55 = 0.33$, not the real $\frac{9}{20} = 0.45$.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

## Device and caffeine: our own joint table

```{ojs}
//| output: false
make_crosstab = (pad) => {
  if (!joint_table.length) return html`<p style="color:#aaa;">Not enough data yet.</p>`
  const devices = [...new Set(joint_table.map(d => d.device))]
  const caffs = [...new Set(joint_table.map(d => d.caffeine))]
  const grandTotal = d3.sum(joint_table, d => d.count)
  const cell = (dev, caf) => joint_table.find(r => r.device === dev && r.caffeine === caf)?.count ?? 0
  const rowTotal = dev => d3.sum(caffs, c => cell(dev, c))
  const colTotal = caf => d3.sum(devices, d => cell(d, caf))
  const p = pad

  return html`<table style="width:80%;margin:0 auto;border-collapse:collapse;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.95em;">
    <caption class="visually-hidden">Number of students by device and caffeine use, with row and column totals.</caption>
    <thead><tr style="background:#1a1a2e;color:white;">
      <th scope="col" style="padding:${p+1}px 18px;text-align:left;">Device \\ Caffeine</th>
      ${caffs.map(c => `<th scope="col" style="padding:${p+1}px 18px;text-align:right;">${c}</th>`).join('')}
      <th scope="col" style="padding:${p+1}px 18px;text-align:right;background:#2d6a4f;">Total</th>
    </tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      ${devices.map((dev,i) => `<tr style="${i%2===1?'background:#fafafa;':''}border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">
        <td style="padding:${p}px 18px;font-weight:700;">${dev}</td>
        ${caffs.map(c => `<td style="padding:${p}px 18px;text-align:right;color:#457b9d;">${cell(dev,c)}</td>`).join('')}
        <td style="padding:${p}px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">${rowTotal(dev)}</td>
      </tr>`).join('')}
      <tr style="border-top:2px solid #1a1a2e;">
        <td style="padding:${p}px 18px;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">Total</td>
        ${caffs.map(c => `<td style="padding:${p}px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#f0f4f8;">${colTotal(c)}</td>`).join('')}
        <td style="padding:${p}px 18px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;background:#e9edf1;">${grandTotal}</td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>`
}
```

```{ojs}
make_crosstab(9)
```

::: {.fragment}
Row and column totals give you the **marginal probabilities** — $P(\text{Device})$ and $P(\text{Caffeine})$, each on its own, ignoring the other variable — directly, with no need to derive them separately before you can condition.
:::

## Task — condition on our own data

```{ojs}
make_crosstab(5)
```

::: {.instructions-box}
On paper, using the table above: what is $P(\text{Caffeine} = \text{Yes} \mid \text{Device} = \text{Phone})$?

Does knowing someone's device change your guess about their caffeine use? How much would you trust that conclusion, given how many observations it's based on?
:::

## Independence and sampling noise

**Independence is not a yes/no question you can answer from a table this small.** Any real sample will show *some* numerical gap between the conditional and marginal probabilities, purely by chance — even when the true population relationship is independence. Telling a real pattern from sampling noise is exactly what Week 2's tools (standard errors, hypothesis tests) are for. With this few observations, "we can't tell yet" is the honest answer, not a verdict either way.

## Visualising with a stacked bar chart

```{ojs}
stacked_data = {
  if (!joint_table.length) return []
  const devices = [...new Set(joint_table.map(d => d.device))]
  return devices.flatMap(dev => {
    const rows = joint_table.filter(d => d.device === dev)
    const tot = d3.sum(rows, d => d.count)
    return rows.map(r => ({ ...r, pct: r.count / tot }))
  })
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  if (!stacked_data.length) return html`<p style="color:#aaa;">Not enough data yet.</p>`
  return accessibleChart(Plot.plot({
    height: 400,
    marginLeft: 60,
    marginBottom: 50,
    style: { fontSize: "15px" },
    x: { label: "Device", tickSize: 0 },
    y: { label: "% within device", percent: true },
    color: { legend: true, label: "Caffeine use", tickFormat: d => d === "Yes" ? "Caffeine" : d === "No" ? "No caffeine" : "Unknown", domain: ["Yes","No","Unknown"], range: ["#e63946","#457b9d","#ccc"] },
    marks: [
      Plot.barY(stacked_data, { x: "device", y: "pct", fill: "caffeine", order: "caffeine" }),
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
    ]
  }), `Stacked bar chart of caffeine use within each device, as a percentage of that device's users: the conditional probability of caffeine given device. ${stacked_data.filter(d => d.caffeine === "Yes").map(d => `${d.device}: ${Math.round(100 * d.pct)}% had caffeine`).join("; ")}.`)
}
```

::: {.fragment}
Stacked to 100% within each device — this shows $P(\text{Caffeine} \mid \text{Device})$ directly, not the raw counts. If the two bars differ, device and caffeine are **associated** in our data.
:::

## Task — flip the condition

::: {.instructions-box}
Same table, the other way round. Calculate:

1. $P(\text{Phone} \mid \text{Caffeine} = \text{Yes})$ — of the caffeine drinkers, what share used a phone?
2. $P(\text{Phone})$ — the share of the whole class who used a phone

Is $P(\text{Phone} \mid \text{Caffeine})$ the same number as $P(\text{Caffeine} \mid \text{Phone})$ from the last task?
:::

```{ojs}
flip = {
  const n = (dev, caf) => d3.sum(joint_table.filter(r => (dev == null || r.device === dev) && (caf == null || r.caffeine === caf)), r => r.count)
  const N = n(null, null)
  return {
    phoneGivenYes: n("Phone","Yes") / n(null,"Yes"),
    pPhone: n("Phone", null) / N,
    yesGivenPhone: n("Phone","Yes") / n("Phone", null),
    nPhoneYes: n("Phone","Yes"), nYes: n(null,"Yes"), nPhone: n("Phone", null), N
  }
}
```

::: {.fragment}
```{ojs}
html`<div style="font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.95em;line-height:1.7;">
  <div>1. P(Phone | Caffeine) = ${flip.nPhoneYes} / ${flip.nYes} = <strong style="color:#e63946;">${flip.phoneGivenYes.toFixed(2)}</strong></div>
  <div>2. P(Phone) = ${flip.nPhone} / ${flip.N} = <strong style="color:#e63946;">${flip.pPhone.toFixed(2)}</strong></div>
  <div style="margin-top:8px;">Compare: P(Caffeine | Phone) = ${flip.nPhoneYes} / ${flip.nPhone} = <strong>${flip.yesGivenPhone.toFixed(2)}</strong></div>
</div>`
```

Same numerator, different denominator — **the order matters.** $P(A \mid B)$ and $P(B \mid A)$ answer different questions.
:::

## What independence would look like

If device and caffeine were **independent**, knowing someone's device would tell you nothing about their caffeine use — every device's bar would look the same as the class overall.

```{ojs}
{
  const caffs = ["Yes","No","Unknown"].filter(c => joint_table.some(r => r.caffeine === c))
  const N = d3.sum(joint_table, r => r.count)
  const overall = Object.fromEntries(caffs.map(c => [c, d3.sum(joint_table.filter(r => r.caffeine === c), r => r.count) / N]))
  const devices = [...new Set(joint_table.map(d => d.device))]
  const rows = [
    ...stacked_data.map(d => ({ ...d, view: "What we observed" })),
    ...devices.flatMap(dev => caffs.map(c => ({ device: dev, caffeine: c, pct: overall[c], view: "If independent" })))
  ]
  return accessibleChart(Plot.plot({
    height: 380,
    width: 900,
    marginLeft: 60,
    marginBottom: 50,
    style: { fontSize: "15px" },
    fx: { label: null, domain: ["What we observed", "If independent"] },
    x: { label: "Device", tickSize: 0 },
    y: { label: "% within device", percent: true },
    color: { legend: true, label: "Caffeine use", tickFormat: d => d === "Yes" ? "Caffeine" : d === "No" ? "No caffeine" : "Unknown", domain: ["Yes","No","Unknown"], range: ["#e63946","#457b9d","#ccc"] },
    marks: [
      Plot.barY(rows, { fx: "view", x: "device", y: "pct", fill: "caffeine", order: "caffeine" }),
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
    ]
  }), "Two pairs of stacked bars side by side. Left: caffeine use within each device, as observed in our class. Right: what the bars would look like if device and caffeine were independent, where every device has the same caffeine share as the class overall. The further apart the two pairs, the more device and caffeine are associated.")
}
```

::: {.fragment}
Independence = **flat bars**: $P(\text{Caffeine} \mid \text{Laptop}) = P(\text{Caffeine} \mid \text{Phone}) = P(\text{Caffeine})$. The further the left-hand bars are from the right-hand ones, the more the two variables depend on each other.
:::

## Task — expected counts if independent {.smaller}

::: {.instructions-box}
If device and caffeine were independent, $P(\text{Phone and Caffeine}) = P(\text{Phone}) \times P(\text{Caffeine})$.

For each of the four cells, calculate the **count** we'd expect under independence:

$$\text{expected count} = N \times P(\text{Device}) \times P(\text{Caffeine}) = \frac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{N}$$

Then compare with the counts we actually observed. Which cells are furthest apart?
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{ojs}
{
  const devices = [...new Set(joint_table.map(d => d.device))]
  const caffs = [...new Set(joint_table.map(d => d.caffeine))]
  const N = d3.sum(joint_table, r => r.count)
  const cell = (dev, caf) => joint_table.find(r => r.device === dev && r.caffeine === caf)?.count ?? 0
  const rowT = dev => d3.sum(caffs, c => cell(dev, c)), colT = caf => d3.sum(devices, d => cell(d, caf))
  return html`<table style="width:85%;margin:8px auto;border-collapse:collapse;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.95em;">
    <caption class="visually-hidden">Observed counts next to the counts expected if device and caffeine were independent.</caption>
    <thead><tr style="background:#1a1a2e;color:white;">
      <th scope="col" style="padding:8px 14px;text-align:left;">Device</th>
      ${caffs.map(c => `<th scope="col" style="padding:8px 14px;text-align:right;">Caffeine: ${c}<br><span style="font-weight:400;font-size:0.85em;">observed / expected</span></th>`).join('')}
    </tr></thead>
    <tbody>${devices.map(dev => `<tr style="border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">
      <td style="padding:8px 14px;font-weight:700;">${dev}</td>
      ${caffs.map(c => `<td style="padding:8px 14px;text-align:right;"><strong style="color:#457b9d;">${cell(dev,c)}</strong> / <span style="color:#e63946;">${(rowT(dev)*colT(c)/N).toFixed(1)}</span></td>`).join('')}
    </tr>`).join('')}</tbody>
  </table>`
}
```

The gaps are small in counts — with ${d3.sum(joint_table, r => r.count)} students, a difference of one or two people per cell is exactly what chance alone produces. Same lesson as before: a table this small can't tell real dependence from noise.
:::

## Conditional distribution and expectation

---

## The conditional mean

The **conditional expectation** of y for a given value of x:

$$E[y \mid x]$$

- The mean of y, computed separately for each value (or group) of x
- With few x values, a histogram or box plot per group works well (Week 1)
- With **many** x values — like finger length in mm — group into **bins** first

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

## Task — what's wrong with our finger-length data?

Before we use it: here are all ${finger_task_rows.length} of our finger-length measurements, anonymised. Something is wrong with **5 of them**. In pairs: find them, and decide what you'd do about it — drop those students, or try to correct the values? If you'd correct them, what would you correct them *to*, and how confident are you?
:::

```{ojs}
{
  const cols = 4
  const rows = finger_task_rows
  const perCol = Math.ceil(rows.length / cols)
  const columns = Array.from({ length: cols }, (_, c) => rows.slice(c * perCol, (c + 1) * perCol))
  return html`<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(${cols},1fr);gap:0 24px;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.9em;margin-top:16px;">
    ${columns.map(col => `<table style="border-collapse:collapse;width:100%;">
      <caption class="visually-hidden">Anonymised finger-length measurements, one column of the full class list.</caption>
      <thead><tr style="border-bottom:2px solid #1a1a2e;">
        <th scope="col" style="text-align:left;padding:4px 8px;">Student</th>
        <th scope="col" style="text-align:right;padding:4px 8px;">mm</th>
      </tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        ${col.map(r => `<tr style="border-bottom:1px solid #eee;">
          <td style="padding:4px 8px;color:#666;">${r.student_name}</td>
          <td style="padding:4px 8px;text-align:right;font-weight:700;">${r.finger_mm}</td>
        </tr>`).join('')}
      </tbody>
    </table>`).join('')}
  </div>`
}
```

## What we'll actually do {.smaller}

::: {.instructions-box}
Two error patterns, not one random mess:
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **Too small** (under 10mm): almost certainly **centimetres entered where millimetres were asked for** — a 6.9 is very plausibly a real 69mm finger, just in the wrong unit
- **Too large** (700–900mm): almost certainly **an extra typed digit** — 900 is very plausibly a real 90mm finger with a stray zero
:::

::: {.fragment}
**We impute, not drop.** Both patterns have an identifiable, high-confidence correction (×10 or ÷10) that lands the value squarely back in the range every other student's real measurement falls in — dropping 5 of 24 students (over 20% of the class) would throw away perfectly good reaction-time data for those students, for a finger-length problem that's actually fixable.
:::

::: {.fragment}
This wouldn't be the right call for every data problem — imputation only makes sense when you have a **specific, well-justified reason** to believe what the correct value should be. A value that's merely unusual, with no diagnosable cause, is a much better candidate for dropping (or for the "keep it, it's a genuine feature of the process" option from Week 1's own three-question framework) than for guessing a replacement.
:::

## Task — compute the conditional mean, by hand

::: {.instructions-box}
Download [**week3_students.csv**](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stevenolanecon/7002LBSAI/main/data/week3_students.csv){style="color:#457b9d;"}: one row per student, with their mean reaction time, their corrected finger length, a **finger_bin** column that already splits the class into three roughly equal groups (Short / Medium / Long), their **device** (Laptop / Phone), and whether they had **caffeine** (Yes / No).

Compute the mean reaction time within each bin (`AVERAGEIF`, or a PivotTable with finger_bin as rows). Compare to the chart on the next slide.
:::

## Binning finger length

::::: {.two-col style="grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; align-items:start;"}
:::: {}
```{ojs}
{
  const rows = student_summary.filter(d => d.finger_mm != null && !isNaN(d.finger_mm))
  if (rows.length < 3) {
    return html`<div class="instructions-box">Not enough finger-length data yet to bin — this will populate once more of the class has submitted through the updated tool.</div>`
  }
  const vals = rows.map(d => d.finger_mm).sort((a,b) => a-b)
  const q1 = d3.quantile(vals, 1/3), q2 = d3.quantile(vals, 2/3)
  const binOf = f => f <= q1 ? "Short" : f <= q2 ? "Medium" : "Long"
  const binned = rows.map(d => ({ ...d, bin: binOf(d.finger_mm) }))
  const grouped = ["Short","Medium","Long"].map(b => {
    const g = binned.filter(d => d.bin === b)
    return { bin: b, n: g.length, mean_rt: g.length ? d3.mean(g, d => d.mean_rt) : null }
  }).filter(g => g.n > 0)
  // Show each bin's range: the two tercile cut points, plus the observed
  // min/max at the ends -- same boundaries pd.qcut produces in the code beside it
  const fmt = v => (+v.toFixed(1)).toString()
  const range = {
    Short:  `${fmt(vals[0])} to ${fmt(q1)} mm`,
    Medium: `>${fmt(q1)} to ${fmt(q2)} mm`,
    Long:   `>${fmt(q2)} to ${fmt(vals[vals.length-1])} mm`,
  }

  return accessibleChart(Plot.plot({
    height: 470,
    width: 560,
    marginLeft: 60,
    marginBottom: 60,
    style: { fontSize: "14px" },
    x: { label: "Finger length bin", domain: ["Short","Medium","Long"], tickFormat: b => `${b}\n${range[b]}` },
    y: { label: "E[reaction time | bin] (ms)" },
    marks: [
      Plot.barY(grouped, { x: "bin", y: "mean_rt", fill: "#457b9d", fillOpacity: 0.8 }),
      Plot.text(grouped, { x: "bin", y: "mean_rt", text: d => `n=${d.n}`, dy: -10, fill: "#333", fontSize: 12 }),
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
    ]
  }), `Bar chart of mean reaction time in each finger-length bin: the conditional mean of reaction time given the bin. ${grouped.map(g => `${g.bin} (${range[g.bin]}): ${Math.round(g.mean_rt)} ms, ${g.n} students`).join("; ")}.`)
}
```
::::

:::: {}
<details>
<summary style="cursor:pointer;color:#2d6a4f;font-size:0.9em;">Show the Python code — how the bins were chosen</summary>

```{ojs}
html`<pre style="font-family:'SF Mono','Menlo',monospace;font-size:0.45em;line-height:1.35;
                  background:#f6f6f8;border:1px solid #e0e0e6;border-radius:6px;
                  padding:8px 14px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;">import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv(data_path)   # week3_reaction_times.csv (one row per trial)

# Decision 1: one row per student, not per trial -- each student's
# finger length is one value, so bin students, not trials
students = (df.groupby('name')
              .agg(mean_rt=('reaction_time_ms', 'mean'),
                   finger=('finger_length_corrected', 'first'))
              .reset_index())

# Decision 2: three bins with roughly equal numbers of students
# (terciles), not equal-width mm ranges -- so no bin ends up nearly empty
students['bin'] = pd.qcut(students['finger'], q=3,
                          labels=['Short', 'Medium', 'Long'])
pd.qcut(students['finger'], q=3).cat.categories   # the cut points

# Decision 3: the conditional mean E[reaction time | bin], plus n per bin
students.groupby('bin', observed=True)['mean_rt'].agg(['mean', 'count'])</pre>`
```

</details>

## Scatterplot and bin-scatter {.smaller}

A **scatterplot** puts two variables on two axes, one dot per observation. It's one of the most powerful ways to see whether a relationship exists between two variables — no formula required, just look.

::: {.fragment}
Not finger length this time — you'll build that scatter yourselves shortly. Here it's a **simulated, illustrative case, not our own class data**: hours of sleep the night before, against reaction time, for 152 made-up trials.
:::

:::: {.shrink-on-reveal data-frag="wk3-scatter-frag" style="--large-height:460px;--small-height:300px;--shrink-scale:0.6522;"}
::: {.shrink-on-reveal-inner}
```{ojs}
{
  return accessibleChart(Plot.plot({
    height: 460,
    marginLeft: 60,
    x: { label: "Sleep the night before (hours)" },
    y: { label: "Reaction time (ms)" },
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(sleep_scatter_data, { x: "sleep_hours", y: "reaction_time_ms", fill: "#457b9d", r: 5, fillOpacity: 0.75,
                       tip: true, title: d => `${d.sleep_hours}h sleep, ${d.reaction_time_ms}ms` }),
    ]
  }), "Scatterplot of simulated reaction time against hours of sleep the night before, one dot per trial. Most trials sit in a tight band that drifts down as sleep increases, but two extremely slow trials stretch the vertical axis and make that pattern hard to see.")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.fragment #wk3-scatter-frag}
Every dot is one trial. There's a real pattern here, but a handful of slow "attention lapse" trials — everyone has them, however well-rested — stretch the top of the scale and make it hard to see. Often with more data this will struggle to fit on a scatter. In those cases, a **bin-scatter** can reveal the pattern without the clutter.
:::

## The bin-scatter

The **conditional mean per bin** — like the finger-length "Short / Medium / Long" buckets, but with more, narrower bins. A bin still needs to be *wide enough to contain several trials* — group by the exact observed sleep value and most bins would only ever hold one trial, which isn't averaging away anything.

:::: {.shrink-on-reveal data-frag="wk3-binscatter-frag" style="--large-height:500px;--small-height:340px;--shrink-scale:0.68;"}
::: {.shrink-on-reveal-inner}
```{ojs}
{
  const width = 1.0
  const grouped = d3.rollups(
      sleep_scatter_data,
      v => ({ mean_rt: d3.mean(v, d => d.reaction_time_ms), n: v.length }),
      d => Math.round(d.sleep_hours / width) * width
    )
    .map(([sleep_hours, { mean_rt, n }]) => ({ sleep_hours, mean_rt, n }))
    .sort((a, b) => a.sleep_hours - b.sleep_hours)

  return accessibleChart(Plot.plot({
    height: 500,
    marginLeft: 60,
    x: { label: "Sleep the night before (hours, 1h bins)" },
    y: { label: "E[reaction time | bin] (ms)" },
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(grouped, { x: "sleep_hours", y: "mean_rt", fill: "#2d6a4f", r: 6, fillOpacity: 0.85,
                       tip: true, title: d => `${d.sleep_hours}h bin (n=${d.n}): ${d.mean_rt.toFixed(0)}ms` }),
      Plot.text(grouped, { x: "sleep_hours", y: "mean_rt", text: d => `n=${d.n}`, dy: -12, fill: "#333", fontSize: 11 }),
    ]
  }), "Bin-scatter of the same simulated data: mean reaction time in each one-hour sleep bin, with the number of trials in each bin labelled. Mean reaction time falls steadily as sleep increases, the pattern the raw scatter hid.")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.fragment #wk3-binscatter-frag}
Every bin here is an average of at least a dozen trials (labelled above each dot) — a lapse trial can still pull a bin's mean up a little, but it can no longer dominate the whole chart the way it did as a single raw point. The downward trend reads far more clearly than in the raw scatter.
:::

## Does logging reaction time help? {.smaller}

Week 1 found reaction time is closer to log-normal than normal — a floor, no ceiling, long right tail. Gabor's own case study logs a skewed variable for exactly this reason: it stretches out the crowded end and compresses the tail, so a pattern against x is easier to read.

```{ojs}
function fitLine(rows, yOf) {
  const xs = rows.map(d => d.sleep_hours), ys = rows.map(yOf)
  const mx = d3.mean(xs), my = d3.mean(ys)
  const b = d3.sum(xs.map((x, i) => (x - mx) * (ys[i] - my))) / d3.sum(xs.map(x => (x - mx) ** 2))
  const a = my - b * mx
  const yhat = xs.map(x => a + b * x)
  const ssRes = d3.sum(ys.map((y, i) => (y - yhat[i]) ** 2))
  const ssTot = d3.sum(ys.map(y => (y - my) ** 2))
  const r2 = 1 - ssRes / ssTot
  const [x0, x1] = d3.extent(xs)
  return { line: [{ x: x0, y: a + b * x0 }, { x: x1, y: a + b * x1 }], r2 }
}
```

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
**Logged**

```{ojs}
{
  const yOf = d => Math.log(d.reaction_time_ms)
  const { line, r2 } = fitLine(sleep_scatter_data, yOf)
  return accessibleChart(Plot.plot({
    height: 340,
    marginLeft: 55,
    x: { label: "Sleep the night before (hours)" },
    y: { label: "ln(reaction time)" },
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(sleep_scatter_data, { x: "sleep_hours", y: yOf, fill: "#2d6a4f", r: 5, fillOpacity: 0.75,
                       tip: true, title: d => `${d.sleep_hours}h sleep, ${d.reaction_time_ms}ms` }),
      Plot.line(line, { x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#1a1a2e", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "5,3" }),
      Plot.text([{ x: line[0].x, y: d3.max(sleep_scatter_data, yOf), label: `R² = ${r2.toFixed(2)}` }],
                { x: "x", y: "y", text: "label", fill: "#2d6a4f", fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 13, textAnchor: "start" }),
    ]
  }), `Scatterplot of logged reaction time against hours of sleep, with a dashed fitted line. On the log scale the downward relationship is clearly visible: R squared is ${r2.toFixed(2)}.`)
}
```
:::
::: {.col .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
**Raw scale**

```{ojs}
{
  const yOf = d => d.reaction_time_ms
  const { line, r2 } = fitLine(sleep_scatter_data, yOf)
  return accessibleChart(Plot.plot({
    height: 340,
    marginLeft: 55,
    x: { label: "Sleep the night before (hours)" },
    y: { label: "Reaction time (ms)" },
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(sleep_scatter_data, { x: "sleep_hours", y: yOf, fill: "#457b9d", r: 5, fillOpacity: 0.75,
                       tip: true, title: d => `${d.sleep_hours}h sleep, ${d.reaction_time_ms}ms` }),
      Plot.line(line, { x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#1a1a2e", strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "5,3" }),
      Plot.text([{ x: line[0].x, y: d3.max(sleep_scatter_data, yOf), label: `R² = ${r2.toFixed(2)}` }],
                { x: "x", y: "y", text: "label", fill: "#457b9d", fontWeight: 700, fontSize: 13, textAnchor: "start" }),
    ]
  }), `Scatterplot of raw reaction time against hours of sleep, with a dashed fitted line. Two extreme trials dominate the vertical axis, so the downward relationship is barely visible: R squared is ${r2.toFixed(2)}.`)
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
Same data, same kind of fitted line, side by side. The lapse trials are still there on both — logging doesn't delete them — but look at what they do to each scale: on the **raw** axis they're so extreme the whole relationship is barely visible (R² ≈ 0.08 — weak). **Logged**, the same two points barely stretch the axis, and the downward trend most students missed on the raw scatter is suddenly obvious (R² ≈ 0.35 — over four times stronger). Logging a skewed variable is a tool, not a rule: it helps here only because it actually improves the fit, and Week 5 goes further into why.
:::

## Covariance

In plain language: **covariance** asks whether x and y tend to move together — when one is above its own average, is the other usually above its average too?

::: {.fragment}
$$Cov[x,y] = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{n-1}$$

- Multiplies each observation's deviation from the x-mean by its deviation from the y-mean, and averages
- Positive when x and y tend to deviate from their means **in the same direction**
- Can be any positive or negative number — units depend on the units of x and y
- Like the SD back in Week 1, this divides by $n-1$, not $n$ — the same small-sample correction, applied here too
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

## Covariance, on our own data

:::: {.two-col style="grid-template-columns: 1.25fr 1fr; align-items:center;"}
::: {}
```{ojs}
{
  const rows = student_summary.filter(d => d.finger_mm != null && !isNaN(d.finger_mm))
  if (rows.length < 3) return html`<div class="instructions-box">Not enough finger-length data yet.</div>`
  const mx = d3.mean(rows, d => d.finger_mm), my = d3.mean(rows, d => d.mean_rt)
  const colored = rows.map(d => ({ ...d, sign: (d.finger_mm - mx) * (d.mean_rt - my) >= 0 ? "Same sign (+)" : "Opposite sign (−)" }))

  return accessibleChart(Plot.plot({
    height: 470,
    width: 620,
    marginLeft: 60,
    marginTop: 30,
    marginRight: 34,
    x: { label: "Finger length (mm)" },
    y: { label: "Mean reaction time (ms)" },
    color: { domain: ["Same sign (+)", "Opposite sign (−)"], range: ["#2d6a4f", "#e63946"], legend: true },
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleX([mx], { stroke: "#1a1a2e", strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "5,4" }),
      Plot.ruleY([my], { stroke: "#1a1a2e", strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "5,4" }),
      Plot.text([mx], { x: d => d, frameAnchor: "top", dy: -14, text: () => "x̄", fontSize: 20, fontWeight: 700, fill: "#1a1a2e" }),
      Plot.text([my], { y: d => d, frameAnchor: "right", dx: 22, text: () => "ȳ", fontSize: 20, fontWeight: 700, fill: "#1a1a2e" }),
      Plot.dot(colored, { x: "finger_mm", y: "mean_rt", fill: "sign", r: 6, fillOpacity: 0.85,
                       tip: true, title: d => `${d.student_name}: ${d.finger_mm}mm, ${d.mean_rt.toFixed(0)}ms` }),
    ]
  }), `Scatterplot of mean reaction time against finger length, with dashed lines at the two means, x-bar and y-bar, dividing it into four quarters. Dots are green where a student is on the same side of both means (a positive contribution to covariance) and red where they are on opposite sides (a negative contribution). ${colored.filter(d => d.sign.startsWith("Same")).length} of ${colored.length} students are green.`)
}
```
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.8em;"}
$$Cov[x,y] = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{n-1}$$

The dashed lines are the two means: **$\bar{x}$** (vertical, mean finger length) and **$\bar{y}$** (horizontal, mean reaction time).

::: {.fragment}
Each point's contribution is $(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})$:

- **Green** — both deviations the same sign, positive product
- **Red** — opposite signs, negative product

Covariance is the average of all these products.
:::
:::
::::

## Task — calculate the covariance

::: {.instructions-box}
In Excel, using **week3_students.csv**: calculate $Cov[\text{finger length}, \text{reaction time}]$.
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{ojs}
{
  const rows = student_summary.filter(d => d.finger_mm != null && !isNaN(d.finger_mm))
  if (rows.length < 3) return html`<p style="color:#aaa;">Will compute automatically once enough data is in.</p>`
  const xs = rows.map(d => d.finger_mm), ys = rows.map(d => d.mean_rt)
  const mx = d3.mean(xs), my = d3.mean(ys)
  const cov = d3.sum(xs.map((x,i) => (x - mx) * (ys[i] - my))) / (xs.length - 1)
  return html`<p style="font-family:sans-serif;">Cov[finger length, reaction time] = <strong style="color:#e63946;font-size:1.2em;">${cov.toFixed(1)}</strong></p>`
}
```
:::

## Correlation

In plain language: **correlation** asks the same question as covariance — do x and y move together — but reports the answer on a fixed scale from −1 to 1, so it's comparable no matter what units x and y are measured in.

Both covariance and correlation measure the direction and strength of a **linear association**. Correlation is the standardised version of the covariance — divide by the product of the standard deviations:

$$Corr[x,y] = \frac{Cov[x,y]}{SD[x] \, SD[y]} \qquad -1 \leq Corr[x,y] \leq 1$$

Rough guide: below 0.2 is weak, above 0.7 is generally strong.

## Task — correlation by hand: five students

::: {.instructions-box}
Same five students. You already have $Cov[x,y] = 8$.

1. Calculate $SD[x]$ and $SD[y]$ — square each deviation from the last task, add them up, divide by $n-1$, take the square root
2. Calculate $Corr[x,y] = \dfrac{Cov[x,y]}{SD[x]\,SD[y]}$
3. Strong, weak, or in between?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Squared deviations: $x$: 16 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 40; $y$: 16 + 0 + 4 + 16 + 4 = 40

$$SD[x] = SD[y] = \sqrt{40/4} = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.16 \qquad Corr[x,y] = \frac{8}{3.16 \times 3.16} = \frac{8}{10} = 0.8$$

Above 0.7 — a strong positive association.
:::

## Task — calculate the correlation

::: {.instructions-box}
Now the whole class: using your class covariance from earlier, and the SD of each variable, calculate the correlation coefficient between finger length and reaction time.
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{ojs}
{
  const rows = student_summary.filter(d => d.finger_mm != null && !isNaN(d.finger_mm))
  if (rows.length < 3) return html`<p style="color:#aaa;">Will compute automatically once enough data is in.</p>`
  const xs = rows.map(d => d.finger_mm), ys = rows.map(d => d.mean_rt)
  const mx = d3.mean(xs), my = d3.mean(ys)
  const cov = d3.sum(xs.map((x,i) => (x - mx) * (ys[i] - my))) / (xs.length - 1)
  const corr = cov / (d3.deviation(xs) * d3.deviation(ys))
  return html`<p style="font-family:sans-serif;">Corr[finger length, reaction time] = <strong style="color:#e63946;font-size:1.2em;">${corr.toFixed(2)}</strong></p>`
}
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
Whatever number comes back — is it strong enough, on its own, to justify HR replacing the real test with a ruler?
:::

## Dependence, mean-dependence, correlation

---

## Three ways x and y can be related

Two variables are **associated** whenever they're not independent. But association comes in different forms:

::: {.fragment}
**Independent** — the whole distribution of y is the same whatever the value of x. Knowing x tells you *nothing* about y.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Mean-dependent** — the *average* of y changes with x: $E[y \mid x]$ isn't flat. This is what covariance and correlation pick up.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Dependent, but not in the mean** — the average of y stays the same, but something else about y changes with x, such as its spread.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Correlation only measures the **linear** part of mean-dependence. So a correlation of zero does **not** mean x and y are unrelated.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

## Task — which of these are independent?

::: {.instructions-box}
For each panel: does knowing x tell you anything about y? And what would you guess the correlation is?
:::

```{ojs}
dep_panels = Object.keys(dep_r)
```

```{ojs}
viewof show_dep_means = Inputs.toggle({ label: "Show the conditional mean, E[y | x]", value: false })
```

```{ojs}
{
  const binW = 0.25
  const means = dep_panels.flatMap(p => {
    const pts = dep_data.filter(d => d.panel === p)
    return d3.groups(pts, d => Math.floor(d.x / binW)).map(([b, g]) => ({ panel: p, x: (b + 0.5) * binW, y: d3.mean(g, d => d.y) }))
      .sort((a, b) => a.x - b.x)
  })
  return accessibleChart(Plot.plot({
    height: 270,
    width: 1100,
    marginLeft: 20,
    style: { fontSize: "15px" },
    fx: { label: null, domain: dep_panels, tickFormat: d => `Panel ${d[0]}` },
    x: { label: null, ticks: [] },
    y: { label: null, ticks: [] },
    marks: [
      Plot.frame({ stroke: "#ddd" }),
      Plot.dot(dep_data, { fx: "panel", x: "x", y: "y", r: 2.5, fill: "#457b9d", fillOpacity: 0.6 }),
      show_dep_means ? Plot.line(means, { fx: "panel", x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#e63946", strokeWidth: 3, curve: "basis" }) : null,
    ]
  }), `Four scatterplots. Panel 1: a round, shapeless cloud of points. Panel 2: points rising in a straight band from left to right. Panel 3: a U-shape, high at both ends and low in the middle. Panel 4: a bow-tie or fan shape, centred on the same level throughout, narrow in the middle and widely spread at both edges.${show_dep_means ? " A red line shows the conditional mean of y across x in each panel: flat in panels 1 and 4, rising in panel 2, U-shaped in panel 3." : ""}`)
}
```

::: {.fragment}
```{ojs}
html`<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(4,1fr);gap:10px;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.75em;line-height:1.35;">
  ${dep_panels.map((p, i) => `<div style="text-align:center;"><strong>${["Independent", "Mean-dependent (linear)", "Mean-dependent (U-shape)", "Spread depends on x"][i]}</strong><br>r = <strong style="color:#e63946;">${Math.abs(dep_r[p]) < 0.005 ? "0.00" : dep_r[p].toFixed(2)}</strong></div>`).join('')}
</div>`
```

Only panel 1 is independent. Panels 3 and 4 have **r = 0**, yet x clearly tells you something about y: in 3 the average changes, in 4 the spread does.
:::

## How they fit together

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 900 380" style="width:66%;display:block;margin:0 auto;font-family:sans-serif;" role="img" aria-label="Three nested boxes. Independent sits inside mean-independent, which sits inside zero correlation. A U-shape is an example with zero correlation that is not mean-independent; a fan shape is mean-independent but not independent.">
  <rect x="10" y="10" width="880" height="360" rx="18" fill="#f0f4f8" stroke="#1a1a2e" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="30" y="45" font-size="22" font-weight="700" fill="#1a1a2e">Zero correlation</text>
  <text x="30" y="72" font-size="16" fill="#555">e.g. the U-shape (panel 3)</text>
  <rect x="250" y="95" width="620" height="255" rx="16" fill="#e3ecf4" stroke="#457b9d" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="270" y="130" font-size="22" font-weight="700" fill="#457b9d">Mean-independent: E[y | x] is flat</text>
  <text x="270" y="157" font-size="16" fill="#555">e.g. the fan (panel 4)</text>
  <rect x="520" y="185" width="330" height="145" rx="14" fill="#d8efe2" stroke="#2d6a4f" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="540" y="225" font-size="22" font-weight="700" fill="#2d6a4f">Independent</text>
  <text x="540" y="252" font-size="16" fill="#555">nothing about y depends on x</text>
  <text x="540" y="276" font-size="16" fill="#555">(panel 1)</text>
</svg>
```

::: {.fragment}
- Independent **→** mean-independent **→** zero correlation. Each inner box is a special case of the one around it.
- **None of it works the other way.** Zero correlation doesn't mean independent, so always look at the scatter as well as the number.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

---

## Is it causal?

---

## Where does the variation in x come from?

Comparison requires **variation** in the conditioning variable — and where that variation comes from matters enormously.

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
**Experimental data**

- A treatment is assigned, often randomly
- Differences in y are attributable to the treatment alone
- e.g. randomly assign aspirin vs. placebo
:::
::: {.col}
**Observational data**

- x varies because of people's own choices, circumstances, history
- Many other things may differ alongside x
- e.g. people who already take aspirin routinely may do so *because* of prior health risk
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Almost everything in business analytics is observational. Finger length is one of the few genuinely fixed, "as-if-random" variables we're likely to find — most x's we'll meet from here on are not.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::

## AI and finding patterns

GenAI is genuinely useful for a first pass over a new dataset — spotting candidate patterns quickly, the way a quick script or profiler would.

::: {.fragment}
Where it's weaker: **judging** whether a correlation is meaningfully weak or strong, and knowing *which* pattern is worth pursuing in the first place. That judgment is still yours.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 4
:::
